source_text: Nam ille Manichaeus, sicut uoluit naturas, quas hic didicit, ordinare in phantasmatibus suis uelut in gente tenebrarum, omnino falsus esse conuincitur. primo quia tenebrae nihil possunt gignere, ut dictum est. sed non, inquit, tales erant illae tenebrae, quales hic nosti. unde ergo me de illis doces? an forte tam uerbosus doctrinae pollicitator cogis, ut credam? sed fac me credere. illud tamen scio, quod si non habebant aliquam speciem, sicut istae non habent, nihil generare potuerunt; si autem habebant, meliores erant. tu autem cum dicis non fuisse tales, quasi peiores aliquas credi cupis. posses dicere etiam silentium, quod sic est auribus ut tenebrae oculis, aliqua ibi surda uel muta animalia genuisse, ut, cum tibi diceretur non esse aliquam naturam silentium, responderes "sed non tale silentium, quale hic nosti," ut omnino quod uelles, diceres eis, quos semel, ut tibi crederent, decepisses. quamquam id, quod eum induxit, ut in tenebris serpentia nata esse confingeret, in ipsis quidem primordiis nascentium potuit bene animaduerti. sed sunt serpentes, qui tam acute uident et sic praesentia lucis exultant, ut grauissimum testimonium contra eum dicere uideantur. deinde in aquis natantia facile fuit hic discernere et ad illa transferre phantasmata; sic et in uentis uolantia, quoniam huius crassioris aeris inpulsus, in quo aues uolitant, uentus dicitur; in igni uero quadrupedia unde illi fingere in mentem uenerit, nescio. et tamen non frustra hoc dixit, sed parum adtendit et errauit nimis. hanc enim solent rationem reddere, quod quadrupedes edaces sint et in concubitum multum ferueant. sed multi homines edacitate sua superant quemlibet quadrupedem, qui certe bipedes sunt, quos non ignis, sed fumi esse filios dicit. anseribus uero non facile quicquam edacius inuenitur; quos siue in fumo ponat, quia bipedes sunt, siue in aquis, quia natare amant, siue in uentis, quia pennati sunt, et interdum uolant: ad ignem certe secundum eius distinctionem non pertinent. quod autem adtinet ad feruorem concubitus, credo eum animaduertisse hinnientes equos et saepe morsis frenis raptos in feminas: quod animaduersum dum uult cito scribere, non adtendit passerem parietinum, in cuius conparatione quiuis admissarius frigidissimus inuenitur. bipedes uero in fumo cum ab eis quaeritur quare ordinauerit, respondent elatum et superbum esse bipedum genus; hinc enim homines trahere originem dicunt; et quoniam fumus globosus et quasi tumidus in auras erigitur, superbis esse similem non absurde adtenderunt. quae animaduersio sufficere debuit ad aliquam similitudinem dandam de superbis hominibus, siue allegoriam uel formandam uel intellegendam; non tamen, ut ideo bipedes animantes in fumo et de fumo nati esse credantur. nam et\' in puluere nasci debuerunt, quia saepe non minore ambitu et elatione surgit in caelum; et in nebulis, quia plerumque de terra ita exhalantur, ut longe intuentibus incertum etiam faciant, fumusne an nebulae sint. postremo cur in aquis et uentis de habitandi patientia ad habitatores ductum est argumentum ? quia uidemus et natantia in aquis et uolantia in uentis uiuere. ignis uero et fumus non deterruit hominem mentientem, ut puderet eum tales ibi habitatores constituere, quibus nihil constitueretur absurdius? nam quadrupedem ignis incendit atque corrumpit et bipedes fumus offocat et necat. uel hinc certe cogitur fateri se meliores dicere in gente tenebrarum istas fuisse naturas, ubi uult omnia peiora credi. siquidem ibi gignebat ignis quadrupedem et nutriebat et continebat innoxie uel etiam commodissime. similiter et fumus bipedes suos clementissimo sinu editos non solum sine molestia, sed uitaliter atque indulgenterusque in illum principatum educauerat et continebat. ita ostenduntur ista mendacia animaduersione rerum, quae uidentur in mundo, sed minus diligenti minusque sollerti ca.rnali sensu concepta et phantasmatis parturita et temeritate edita atque conscripta haereticorum numerum auxisse.
thought_title: Mani's beasts in the darkness refuted
orientation: Augustine is speaking, refuting Mani's arrangement of crawling, swimming, flying, four-footed and two-footed creatures in the land of darkness.
pass_a_gloss: For that Mani, as he wanted to arrange the natures which he learned here in his fantasies as if in the race of darkness, is proved to be wholly false. First because darkness can beget nothing, as has been said. But not, he says, such were those darknesses as you know here. From where then do you teach me about them? Or perchance as so wordy a promiser of teaching do you compel me to believe? But suppose you make me believe. That however I know, that if they did not have any form, just as these here do not have, they could beget nothing; but if they had, they were better. You however when you say they were not such, you desire as if some worse things to be believed. You could say also that silence, which is to ears as darkness is to eyes, begot there some deaf or mute living things, so that, when it should be said to you that silence is not any nature, you would answer but not such silence as you know here, so that entirely what you wished you would say to those whom you had once deceived so that they would believe you. Although that which led him to invent that crawling things were born in darkness could indeed have been well observed in the very beginnings of newborns. But there are serpents which see so keenly and so rejoice in the presence of light that they seem to speak the weightiest testimony against him. Then the swimming things in the waters were easy to discern here and to transfer to those fantasies; and so also the flying things in the winds, since the thrust of this thicker air in which birds fly is called wind; but in fire from where it came into his mind to invent four-footed things, I do not know. And yet not without reason he said this, but he paid little attention and erred greatly. For they are accustomed to give this reason, that four-footed animals are voracious and burn much toward mating. But many men surpass with their voracity any four-footed animal, who certainly are two-footed, whom he says are sons not of fire but of smoke. But than geese nothing is easily found more voracious; which whether he puts in smoke, because they are two-footed, or in waters, because they love to swim, or in winds, because they are feathered, and sometimes they fly: to fire certainly according to his distinction they do not belong. But as to what pertains to the heat of mating, I believe he observed neighing horses and often snatched toward females with bitten bridles: which observation while he wants to write quickly, he did not observe the house sparrow, in comparison with which any stallion is found most cold. But as to two-footed things in smoke, when it is asked of them why he arranged it, they answer that the race of two-footed things is lifted up and proud; for from this they say men draw origin; and since smoke rounded and as if swollen rises into the breezes, they observed not absurdly that it is similar to proud men. Which observation ought to have sufficed for giving some likeness about proud men, whether for forming an allegory or for understanding one; not however so that therefore two-footed living things should be believed to be in smoke and born from smoke. For they ought also to have been born in dust, because often with no less circling and lifting it rises to heaven; and in mists, because generally they are so breathed out from earth that they make it uncertain even to those looking from afar whether they are smoke or mists. Finally why in waters and winds was the argument led from the endurance of dwelling to the dwellers? Because we see both swimming things live in waters and flying things live in winds. Did fire truly and smoke not deter the lying man so that he would be ashamed to establish such dwellers there, than whom nothing more absurd would be established? For fire burns and corrupts the four-footed animal and smoke chokes and kills the two-footed. From this at least certainly he is compelled to confess that he says those natures in the race of darkness were better, where he wants all things to be believed worse. Since there fire was begetting the four-footed and was nourishing and containing it harmlessly or even most commodiously. Likewise also smoke had raised and was containing its two-footed brought forth in a most merciful bosom not only without trouble but vitally and indulgently even to that princedom. Thus those lies are shown to have been conceived by an observation of things which are seen in the world, but less diligent and less skillful with carnal sense, and brought forth with fantasies, and uttered and written with rashness, and to have increased the number of heretics.

pass_b_english: Mani stands exposed as wholly false in his wish to arrange the natures he learned here in his fantasies, as if into a race of darkness. First, darkness can beget nothing, as I have said.

He answers, "Those darknesses were not like the darkness you know here." From where, then, do you teach me about them? Or do you, so wordy a promiser of teaching, perhaps force me to believe? Suppose I believe him. I still know this much. If those darknesses had no form, just as the darkness here has none, they could generate nothing. If they had form, they were better. Yet when he says they were not like these, he wants us to believe in something worse. He might as well say that silence, which is to the ears what darkness is to the eyes, begot deaf or mute animals there. Then, when told that silence is no nature, he would answer, "But not the kind of silence you know here." In that way you would say whatever you pleased to those you had once tricked into believing you.

Although what led him to invent crawling creatures born in darkness could indeed have been well noticed in the very first stirrings of newborn creatures. But some serpents see sharply and exult so much in the presence of light that they seem to testify heavily against him. It was easy to discern swimming creatures here in the waters and transfer fantasies to them, and so too with flying creatures in the winds, since we call the push of this thicker air, where birds fly, wind. Why it entered his mind to invent four-footed animals in fire, I do not know. He did not say it without a reason, but he paid too little heed and went badly wrong. His followers usually give this reason. Four-footed animals are voracious and burn strongly for mating. But many men outdo any four-footed animal in voracity, and men are certainly two-footed, and Mani calls them sons not of fire but of smoke.

Nothing is readily found more voracious than geese. He may place them in smoke because they have two feet, or in the waters because they love to swim, or in the winds because they have feathers and sometimes fly. By his own division they certainly do not belong to fire. On burning for mating, I think he watched neighing horses drag toward mares with bitten bridles. He rushed to write down what he saw and ignored the house sparrow. Beside that sparrow any stallion looks icy cold.

When asked why Mani put two-footed creatures in smoke, they answer that the race of two-footed creatures is lofty and proud. Men draw their origin from there, they say. Smoke rises into the air in a ball and seems swollen, so they judged it not absurdly like the proud. That observation could have served to supply a likeness of proud men, to frame an allegory or grasp one. It should not make us believe that two-footed living creatures were born in smoke and from smoke. By the same logic they should have been born in dust, for dust often rises to the sky with no less swirl and lift. They should have been born in mists, for mists often breathe up from the earth so that watchers far off cannot tell smoke from mist.

Finally, why draw the argument in waters and winds from the fact that dwelling can be endured to the dwellers? We see swimming creatures live in the waters and flying creatures live in the winds. Did fire and smoke not check this liar with shame? He set such dwellers there that nothing more absurd could be set. Fire burns a four-footed animal and corrupts it, and smoke chokes two-footed creatures and kills them. By this fact alone he must admit that he makes those natures better in the race of darkness, where he wants us to believe all is worse. There fire begot the four-footed animal and fed it and kept it safely, even comfortably. Likewise smoke bore its own two-footed children from a most gentle fold and raised them without trouble, with life-giving care, all the way to that princedom, and kept them there. So these lies stand exposed by the things we see in the world. They were conceived by a careless and unskilled fleshly sense, labored out by fantasies, and rashly uttered and written down, and they have swelled the number of heretics.

problems.quote: I can see what led him to invent crawling creatures born in darkness. He watched newborn things at their very beginnings.
problems.source_quote: id, quod eum induxit, ut in tenebris serpentia nata esse confingeret, in ipsis quidem primordiis nascentium potuit bene animaduerti
problems.why: The source says the cause could be well observed in the very beginnings of things being born, a concessive point. The English recasts it as Augustine's own claim and misplaces the observer.
problems.fix: Yet what led him to invent serpents born in darkness could well be noticed in the very first beginnings of things being born.

problems.quote: Does this wordy promiser of teaching only force me to believe?
problems.source_quote: an forte tam uerbosus doctrinae pollicitator cogis, ut credam?
problems.why: The source is an address to Mani, 'do you, so wordy a promiser of teaching, perhaps compel me to believe?', not a third-person statement. 'Only' is added.
problems.fix: Or do you, such a wordy promiser of teaching, simply compel me to believe?
problems.ruling: cogis is 2nd-person address; an forte is not 'only.' English shifts to third person and adds 'only.'

edits.old: I can see what led him to invent crawling creatures born in darkness. He watched newborn things at their very beginnings.
edits.new: Although what led him to invent crawling creatures born in darkness could indeed have been well noticed in the very first stirrings of newborn creatures.

edits.old: Does this wordy promiser of teaching only force me to believe?
edits.new: Or do you, so wordy a promiser of teaching, perhaps force me to believe?

fixed: Concessive passive restored: 'quamquam ... potuit bene animaduerti' means it could have been observed, not that Augustine saw it or Mani watched it.
Second-person address restored: 'cogis' with 'forte' means 'do you compel', not third-person statement; removed added 'only'.

problems.quote: In that way he says whatever he pleases to those he has already tricked into believing him.
problems.source_quote: ut omnino quod uelles, diceres eis, quos semel, ut tibi crederent, decepisses.
problems.why: A hypothetical result (you would say; you would have deceived) is stated as accomplished fact.
problems.fix: In that way you would say whatever you pleased to those you had once tricked into believing you.
problems.ruling: 'diceres... decepisses' is hypothetical (you would say to those you had deceived); English states it as actual fact 'he says', altering the modality.

problems.quote: His followers may place them in smoke because they have two feet
problems.source_quote: quos siue in fumo ponat, quia bipedes sunt
problems.why: Ponat continues Mani (dicit), not the followers who only give the reason.
problems.fix: He may place them in smoke because they have two feet
problems.ruling: 'ponat' has Mani as subject (continues 'dicit'); 'His followers may place them' misattributes the action, changing who is speaking.

problems.quote: two-footed living creatures live in smoke and were born from smoke
problems.source_quote: bipedes animantes in fumo et de fumo nati esse credantur
problems.why: The Latin claims they were born in smoke and from smoke, not that they live there.
problems.fix: two-footed living creatures were born in smoke and from smoke
problems.ruling: 'in fumo et de fumo nati esse' means born in and from smoke; English 'live in smoke' drops the claim about birth in smoke.

problems.quote: Did fire and smoke not check this liar with shame?
problems.source_quote: ignis uero et fumus non deterruit hominem mentientem, ut puderet eum
problems.why: Source is a question: did fire and smoke not deter the lying man so that he felt shame in setting such dwellers; roughly correct, but 'why draw argument' clause garbled.
problems.fix: Did fire and smoke not deter the lying man, so that he was ashamed to set up such dwellers?
problems.ruling: non deterruit...ut puderet states fire and smoke did not shame him; the rhetorical question reverses that.

edits.old: In that way he says whatever he pleases to those he has already tricked into believing him.
edits.new: In that way you would say whatever you pleased to those you had once tricked into believing you.

edits.old: His followers may place them in smoke because they have two feet
edits.new: He may place them in smoke because they have two feet

edits.old: two-footed living creatures live in smoke and were born from smoke
edits.new: two-footed living creatures were born in smoke and from smoke

fixed: modality: fixed to second-person hypothetical 'you would say... you had once tricked... you' for 'quod uelles, diceres... decepisses... tibi'.
agency: fixed to 'He may place' for 'ponat', continuing Mani as subject of 'dicit', not his followers.
mistranslation in fumo et de fumo nati: fixed to 'were born in smoke and from smoke', removing 'live'.

no edit: 'Did fire and smoke not check this liar with shame?' already renders 'ignis uero et fumus non deterruit hominem mentientem, ut puderet eum'; check=deter and with shame=ut puderet is literary, not a misstatement.

problems.quote: It was easy for him to notice swimming creatures here in the water and carry them over into his fantasies. He did the same with flying creatures in the winds
problems.source_quote: deinde in aquis natantia facile fuit hic discernere et ad illa transferre phantasmata; sic et in uentis uolantia
problems.why: He transfers fantasies onto those creatures or regions. The creatures are not carried into the fantasies.
problems.fix: Next, it was easy here to discern swimmers in the water and transfer fantasies to them, and the same with flyers in the winds.
problems.ruling: "ad illa transferre phantasmata": he transfers the creatures to those fantasies/regions. 'Carry them over into his fantasies' is acceptable, but ambiguity is minor; not major.

problems.quote: He answers, "Those darknesses were not like the darkness you know here." Then how does he teach me about them?
problems.source_quote: sed non, inquit, tales erant illae tenebrae, quales hic nosti. unde ergo me de illis doces?
problems.why: This is the imagined interlocutor, addressed as you. After Mani as subject, "he" reads as Mani teaching.
problems.fix: But he says, "Those darknesses were not like the darkness you know here." From where, then, do you teach me about them?
problems.ruling: "sed non, inquit... quales hic nosti. unde ergo me de illis doces?": after Mani is the subject, 'he answers' and 'how does he teach me' leave the speaker unclear, and 'you' is Mani.

problems.quote: Mani stands exposed as wholly false in the way he arranged the natures he learned here into his fantasies, as if into a race of darkness.
problems.source_quote: omnino falsus esse conuincitur. primo quia tenebrae nihil possunt gignere
problems.why: Source gives 'primo' as first ground of refutation; English drops 'first' and makes 'Darkness can beget nothing' a loose aside; also 'sicut uoluit' becomes 'in the way he'.
problems.fix: Mani is proved wholly false in his wish to arrange the natures he learned here in his fantasies, as in a race of darkness. First, darkness can beget nothing, as I said.
problems.ruling: primo quia marks the first ground of conuincitur; English drops both. sicut uoluit ordinare is 'as he wished to arrange,' not 'in the way he arranged.'

fixed: sicut uoluit / primo quia: fixed to 'in his wish to arrange' and restored 'First' — sicut uoluit is wish, primo is first ground.
unde ergo me de illis doces?: fixed to 'do you teach me' — doces is 2nd singular addressed to imagined interlocutor, not Mani teaching.
ad illa transferre phantasmata: fixed direction — discernere here and transfer fantasies ad illa, not carry creatures into fantasies.

last_rejected.quote: So these lies stand exposed by the things we see in the world. They were conceived by a careless and unskilled fleshly sense, labored out by fantasies, and rashly uttered and written down, and they have swelled the number of heretics.
last_rejected.source_quote: ita ostenduntur ista mendacia animaduersione rerum, quae uidentur in mundo, sed minus diligenti minusque sollerti ca.rnali sensu concepta et phantasmatis parturita et temeritate edita atque conscripta haereticorum numerum auxisse.
last_rejected.why: The lies are shown to have multiplied heretics, conceived by a careless observation of visible things and by fleshly sense. Visible things are not what expose them.
last_rejected.fix: So these lies are shown to have swelled the number of heretics: conceived by a less than careful and less than shrewd look at what is seen in the world, by fleshly sense, brought forth by fantasies, and rashly published and written down.
last_rejected.ruling: The English reads the source fine: 'ostenduntur ista mendacia animaduersione rerum, quae uidentur in mundo' = exposed by observation of visible things; the participles 'concepta...auxisse' are rendered correctly.
